readerTitle: Both pizza shops got busier. Both earned less.
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (피자 가게, 헬스장 예약 앱) + 가상 적용 (이사 업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 경쟁자가 바로 따라 할 수 있는 가격 인하는 손님을 빼앗아 오지 못한다. 결국 두 회사의 돈을 손님에게 넘겨줄 뿐이다.
misconception: 경쟁자가 가격을 내리면 똑같이 내리거나 더 내려야 손님을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: 경쟁 전략과 게임 이론의 표준 개념 (가격 전쟁, 죄수의 딜레마)

factChecks.note: 7번 카드의 '경쟁자와 가격을 합의하는 것은 많은 나라에서 불법'은 일반적인 경고입니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 문구를 일반적으로 유지했습니다.

cards.title: Both pizza shops got busier. Both earned less.
body: Two pizza shops face each other across a busy street. One drops its price by $2. The other answers.
Two months later, both kitchens are busier than ever. Both owners are taking home less money. Neither one wanted this, and neither knows how to stop.

image.label: Two pizza shops across a street with falling price signs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 길을 사이에 두고 마주 보는 피자 가게 두 곳. 양쪽 창문의 가격표가 $12 → $10 → $9로 점점 내려가는 모습을 겹쳐서 표현. 두 주인이 서로를 노려보는 코믹한 표정. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your rival just cut prices.
body: You and the shop across the street each sell about 1,000 large pizzas a week at $12. Ingredients and the box cost you $5 a pizza.
This morning your rival put up a sign: large pizzas now $10. What do you do?

options.text: Match it today at $10 so no one leaves
options.feedback: You protect your customers, but each pizza now leaves $5 instead of $7. And you've shown your rival that every cut will be answered.

options.text: Go to $9 and win the street
options.feedback: You may win customers for a week. Then your rival can drop to $9 too, and you're both earning even less than before.

options.text: Hold at $12 for now, watch who actually leaves, and push what they can't copy fast
options.feedback: You risk losing some price-hunting customers for a while. In return you keep your margin and avoid starting a cycle that is hard to stop.

cards.title: Two rounds later.
body: Say you matched at $10. A month later the rival went to $9, and you matched again. Lower prices drew a few new diners, but mostly the two shops just traded the same customers back and forth.

groups.label: Money left after ingredients each week, per shop

cards.callout: Sales up 10%. Money left after ingredients down about 37%.

cards.title: Price war
body: A **price war** is when rivals answer each price cut with a cut of their own, round after round.

The key idea: a price cut wins customers only if rivals *don't* match it. When they can match quickly, each business keeps roughly the same share. The only lasting change is that customers pay less and every business keeps less.

image.label: Two arrows pushing the price down in a loop
image.brief: 순환 다이어그램. "You cut" → "They match" → "Same share" → "Less money for both" → 다시 "You cut"으로 이어지는 원형 화살표. 가운데에 아래로 내려가는 가격 그래프 아이콘.

cards.title: In software, the war moves in hours.
body: Two booking apps for gyms each charge $50 a month per location. Servers, payment fees and support cost about $8, so each location leaves $42.
One app cuts to $35. The rival updates its pricing page that afternoon. Now each location leaves $27, about 36% less.
Two things make digital wars worse. Changing a price takes minutes, so matching is instant. And current users ask for the new price at renewal, so the cut hits **every customer**, not just new ones.

image.label: Two pricing pages changing on the same day
image.brief: 노트북 화면 두 개가 나란히 있고, 각 요금제 페이지의 "$50/month"가 같은 날 "$35/month"로 바뀌는 모습. 화면 위에 시계 아이콘(오전 → 오후). 실제 서비스 로고나 UI는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Why smart owners walk into it.
body: Each owner thinks: if I don't cut, I lose customers. If I cut and they don't, I win. Either way, cutting looks right.
Both owners think the same way, so both cut, and both end up worse off. Game theory calls this pattern a **prisoner's dilemma**.
list: Compete on what's hard to copy fast: speed, quality, service, location
Respond narrowly, only where customers are truly at risk
Don't start a war you can't outlast

cards.title: Sometimes the lower price is real.
body: If a rival's costs are truly lower, its lower price isn't a bluff. Holding your price may slowly lose customers, and you need a different answer than waiting.
The reverse is also true. A business with a real cost advantage can cut on purpose, because rivals can't match without losing money.
One more line not to cross: agreeing with competitors to keep prices up is illegal in many countries. The way out of a war is your own choices, not a deal with a rival.

cards.title: Now it's a moving company.
body: You run a local moving company known for showing up on time and handling furniture with care. A rival starts advertising 30% off every move this season.

options.text: Advertise 30% off too, starting next week
options.feedback: You keep the price-shoppers, but every move now earns 30% less. And the rival can go to 35% tomorrow.

options.text: Keep your prices and sell what the rival can't match quickly: guaranteed arrival times and damage cover
options.feedback: You may lose some bargain hunters. You keep your margin and the customers who care most about a safe, on-time move.

options.text: Quietly match the rival only for customers who show you its quote
options.feedback: This limits the damage to a few jobs. But word spreads, and soon every customer arrives with a rival's quote in hand.

cards.title: A cut your rival can copy wins you nothing.
body: When competitors can match quickly, price cuts don't move customers. They move money from every business to the customer. Compete where copying is slow.
**Try it today:** write down what your closest rival could copy in one day, and what would take them a year. Put your effort into the second list.
